interviewQuestions.question: Walk me through reversing a singly linked list in place, and explain why your approach uses constant extra space.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I keep three references alive as I walk the list once: `prev` (the reversed portion's new head, starting null), `curr` (the node I'm rewiring), and a temporary `next` that I save before I touch anything.

Each step does four things in a fixed order: save `curr.next` into `next` first — this is the step people skip and then lose the rest of the list — then point `curr.next` back at `prev`, then advance `prev` to `curr`, then advance `curr` to the saved `next`. Repeat until `curr` is null; `prev` is the new head.

It's O(n) time because I touch each node exactly once, and O(1) space because I only ever hold three pointers, regardless of list length — no array, no recursion stack, no auxiliary structure. That's the detail I'd contrast with the recursive version of the same problem, which is elegant to read but spends O(n) stack frames, one per node, which absolutely counts as extra space even though there's no explicit container.

I'd also mention that this exact three-pointer pattern is the backbone for every other reversal variant — sublist reversal and k-group reversal are the same walk with different start/stop conditions, not new algorithms.

**Testing:** whether you can execute the pointer choreography cleanly and correctly identify the true space cost, not just recite "O(1) space" by memory.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Fundamentals

interviewQuestions.question: How would you reverse only the nodes between positions left and right in a singly linked list, in one pass?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The key extra step versus a full reversal is finding the node **just before** position `left`, because that's the only anchor I have for reconnecting afterward — I can't walk backward once I'm inside the sublist.

I use a dummy head so position 1 isn't a special case, then walk `left - 1` steps from the dummy to reach that anchor node, call it `before`. From `before.next`, I run the standard three-pointer reversal, but stop after exactly `right - left + 1` steps instead of running to the end of the list.

Two reconnections finish it: `before.next` now needs to point at the new head of the reversed segment, which is whatever `prev` holds when the loop stops. And the **original `left` node**, which is now the segment's tail, needs its `next` pointed at whatever node the loop's `curr` landed on after the last swap — the first untouched node past `right`.

The dummy head is what makes this uniform: without it, reversing starting exactly at position 1 needs different reconnection code than reversing from the middle, because there's no real predecessor node to anchor `before` on.

**Testing:** whether you can extend the base reversal pattern to a bounded region without introducing an extra pass or extra space.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Technique

interviewQuestions.question: What's the trickiest part of reversing a list in groups of k, and how do you avoid it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The trickiest part isn't reversing a single group — that's the same three-pointer walk as always. It's the **seam between groups**: making sure a reversed group's original first node, now its tail, correctly reconnects to whatever comes next, and correctly handling a final group that's shorter than k.

My approach: before reversing a group, walk k steps ahead to confirm k nodes actually exist. If they don't, I leave that remainder untouched and return — reversing a partial group and having nothing valid to join it to would corrupt the list rather than error cleanly, which makes it a dangerous silent bug.

Once I know a full group exists, I reverse it with the standard walk, then explicitly wire the group's original first node (now the tail) to the result of recursively processing the rest of the list. I return the group's original last node (now the head) up to whoever called this group's reversal, so the join happens one level up automatically.

A concrete failure mode I watch for: forgetting that reconnection step entirely leaves the reversed group's tail pointing at a stale node from inside its own group — the list looks reversed group-by-group in isolation but is actually broken end-to-end.

**Testing:** whether you can reason about multi-segment pointer rewiring, not just single-pass reversal.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Edge cases

interviewQuestions.question: Why would you pick the iterative reversal over the recursive one in a production system handling long lists?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Because the recursive version's elegance hides a real cost: it uses one stack frame per node, so a list of a few hundred thousand elements can hit a language's recursion depth limit or blow the call stack entirely — a failure mode that doesn't show up on the small test cases you'd typically hand-check in an interview.

The iterative version does the identical logical work — same three pointers, same rewiring — using O(1) auxiliary space regardless of list length. There's no asymptotic time difference; both are O(n). The entire argument is about space, and specifically about a kind of space (stack depth) that's invisible unless you think to ask "where does this recursion's memory live?"

In a real system I'd also weigh that stack overflows tend to be ungraceful failures — a crash or an unhandled exception — versus an iterative version that simply keeps running, so the risk profile matters more than the constant-factor overhead of function calls.

If the language or runtime doesn't guarantee tail-call optimization (Python and Java don't; some Scheme/Erlang runtimes do), that risk is real, not theoretical, so I'd default to iterative unless the list length is provably bounded small.

**Testing:** whether you connect an abstract space-complexity claim to a concrete production failure mode.
